Short case 10 · General Surgery

Ulcer

The case that is won at the edge. Describe five things in order, name the edge, and the diagnosis usually names itself. Everything else is confirmation.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1Definition and parts

Definition
SRB: "Ulcer is disruption or break in the continuity of any lining, may be skin, mucous membrane or others. Ulcer is one of the types of wounds."​SRB 1 · p.1
The five things to describe, in this order
Site · size and shape · edge · floor · base. SRB's figure names the parts as floor and base.​SRB 1 · p.15 Then the surrounding skin, the discharge, and the regional lymph nodes.
Edge is not margin
S Das is explicit: "The term 'edge' should not be confused with the term 'margin'."​Das 4 · p.63 The margin is the junction of normal skin with the ulcer; the edge is the area between the margin and the floor, and it is the edge that carries the diagnosis.
Floor is not base
The floor is what you can see, the exposed surface of the ulcer.​Das 4 · p.64 The base is what the ulcer rests on, which may be bone or soft tissue, and it is palpated.​SRB 1 · p.15​Das 4 · p.64 Saying which you mean, and palpating the base rather than only looking at the floor, is the single commonest thing candidates get wrong.
The five edges, with the mechanism of each This is the heart of the case, and SRB supplies not just the list but the pathology behind each.​SRB 1 · p.15​Das 4 · p.64

1. Sloping edge: a healing ulcer. S Das describes the three zones from the centre outwards: red granulation tissue, then a blue zone of thin growing epithelium, then a white zone of scar.​Das 4 · p.64 SRB: the middle part is blue due to epithelial proliferation.​SRB 1 · p.15 Also the edge of a venous ulcer once it granulates well.​SRB 1 · p.27
2. Undermined edge: tuberculous. The reason: "disease process advances in deeper plane, in subcutaneous tissue, whereas the epidermis proliferates inwards".​SRB 1 · p.15 S Das's bedside proof: a probe can be easily insinuated between the edge and the floor of the ulcer.​Das 4 · p.63
3. Punched out edge: gummatous, that is syphilitic, and trophic. The reason: endarteritis.​SRB 1 · p.15 The tissue dies in a block because its artery died, so the edge drops vertically.
4. Raised and beaded, pearly-white edge: rodent ulcer, that is basal cell carcinoma.​SRB 1 · p.15​Das 4 · p.64
5. Everted or rolled-out edge: squamous cell carcinoma. S Das gives the mechanism: the ulcer heaps up and spills over the normal skin to produce an everted edge.​Das 4 · p.64

And the spreading ulcer, which is a sixth appearance: the edge is inflamed, irregular and oedematous.​SRB 1 · p.16​Das 4 · p.63

2Clinical classification, which is what you report

SpreadingHealingChronic / callous
EdgeInflamed, irregular, oedematousSloping Indolent, often thickened
Floor No healthy granulation; profuse purulent discharge and slough Healthy pink or red granulation; scanty serous discharge, no slough Unhealthy, pale, flat granulation
SurroundingsRed and oedematousNo inflammation Fibrosed
Lymph nodesEnlarged and tender May be enlarged, but always non-tenderVariable
PainAcutely painfulSettlingUsually painless

SRB ch.1 pp.16, 19. The tender-versus-non-tender node is the discriminator worth memorising: tender nodes mean active infection, non-tender enlarged nodes in a healing ulcer mean reactive hyperplasia, and non-tender hard fixed nodes mean something else entirely.

Pathological classification
Specific: tuberculous, syphilitic, actinomycotic. Malignant: carcinomatous, rodent (BCC), melanotic. Non-specific: traumatic, which may be mechanical, physical or chemical and is the commonest; arterial, from atherosclerosis or thromboangiitis obliterans; venous or gravitational; trophic or neuropathic; and the ulcers of systemic disease, which SRB lists as anaemia, polycythaemia, sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, leukaemia, vasculitis and autoimmune disease.​SRB 1 · p.17, p.29 S Das's two axes are the same: clinical and pathological.​Das 4 · p.68
Site is a diagnosis in itself
S Das's map: cutaneous tuberculosis on the face, fingers and hand, with lupus vulgaris on the face; Hunterian chancre and soft sores on the external genitalia; gummatous ulcers over subcutaneous bones such as tibia, sternum and skull; perforating or trophic ulcers on the heel or the ball of the foot, which carries maximum body weight; and malignant ulcers anywhere but commonly on the lips, tongue, breast, penis and anus.​Das 4 · p.63
The venous ulcer's site, preciselySRB: vertically oval, commonly on the medial side, occasionally lateral, often both sides of the ankle, but never above the middle third of the leg.​SRB 1 · p.27 That "never above the middle third" is a discriminator you can state as a rule.
Induration, and where to feel for it
SRB: "Induration is a clinical palpatory sign which means there is a specific type of hardness in the diseased tissue. It is obvious in well-differentiated carcinomas. It is better felt in squamous cell" carcinoma.​SRB 1 · p.15 So palpate the base and the margin between finger and thumb, and report induration as a separate finding from the edge.
Three granulation tissues, and what each means Healthy, pink or red, flat granulation: a healing ulcer.​SRB 1 · p.16
Unhealthy, pale, flat granulation: a chronic non-healing or callous ulcer.​SRB 1 · p.19
Exuberant granulation, "proud flesh": granulation protruding out of the ulcer bed or sinus opening like a proliferating mass, and SRB gives the reason it matters: "It is commonly associated with a retained foreign body." It "should be scooped out using Volkmann's scoop prior to skin grafting". A pyogenic granuloma is a type of it: a well-localised red swelling that bleeds on touching.​SRB 1 · p.19

So proud flesh is not just an appearance, it is a prompt to look for a foreign body.

3History, the five questions that matter

How did it start, and how long ago?
S Das: duration is the second thing to establish. And ask about trauma, because an ulcer may follow a burn, and about the scar: "Sometimes a malignant ulcer (Marjolin's) may develop on the scar of a burn."​Das 4 · p.61
Is it painful?
A spreading ulcer is acutely painful; a healing one settles; a chronic callous ulcer is usually painless.​SRB 1 · p.16, p.19 SRB on the venous ulcer: "Ulcer is initially painful; but once chronicity develops it becomes painless."​SRB 1 · p.27 And tuberculous ulcers "are usually painless".​SRB 1 · p.17
SoPainlessness does not mean benign; in this case it means either chronic, tuberculous, or neuropathic.
Is the sensation normal around it?
Because a trophic ulcer is a neuropathic one. S Das's example is a trophic ulcer at the heel resulting from nerve injury, with the scar of the injury visible.​Das 4 · p.63 SRB illustrates bilateral trophic ulceration of the feet due to anaesthesia in leprosy.​B&L 6 · p.80 In India, test sensation in every foot ulcer.
Any varicose veins, claudication, or diabetes?
Because the three commonest chronic leg ulcers are venous, arterial and neuropathic, and the history separates them before you look.
Any contact with tuberculosis, or weight loss and evening fever?
Because a tuberculous ulcer has an undermined edge and needs drugs, not excision. SRB's management: discharge study, biopsy and later antituberculous drugs.​SRB 1 · p.17
Does Marjolin's ulcer metastasise? SRB 1 p.24 says it does not spread by lymphatics or blood; B&L 45 p.652 makes no such claim
SRB
"Marjolin's ulcer can occur in an unstable scar of long duration usually after burns or snake bite. It is well differentiated SCC which does not spread through lymphatics or blood."​SRB 1 · p.24 Its treatment is wide local excision with skin grafting, with regional lymph node block dissection reserved for ordinary squamous carcinoma.​SRB 1 · p.24
Bailey & Love 28e
Gives only the definition: "When a SCC appears in a scar it is known as a Marjolin's ulcer." Its eponym footnote records that Marjolin "described the development of carcinomatous ulcers in scars in 1828".​B&L 45 · p.652 It makes no claim at all that such a tumour behaves differently, and it lists scars among the risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma alongside sun exposure, chronic wounds and immunosuppression.​B&L 45 · p.652
Live difference, and the classical claim needs stating with its reason rather than as a fact, because the reason is what makes it defensible and also shows its limits.

Answer: "Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing unstable scar, classically a burn scar. The classical teaching is that it is well differentiated and slow to metastasise, because the scar is relatively avascular and alymphatic, so there is no route for early lymphatic spread. That is why the Indian texts say it does not spread by lymphatics. But it is still a squamous carcinoma: once it grows beyond the scar into normally vascularised tissue it can metastasise, and Bailey and Love 28e makes no exception for it. So I would treat it as a squamous cell carcinoma, by wide local excision with grafting, and I would examine and follow up the regional nodes rather than assume they are safe."​SRB 1 · p.24​B&L 45 · p.652

Giving the mechanism, the scar's poor lymphatic drainage, is what earns the mark; repeating "it does not metastasise" as a bare assertion is what loses it.

4Investigations

Biopsy, and from where
From the edge, including a margin of adjacent normal skin, not from the floor, which is slough and granulation. In a suspected malignant ulcer take an adequate wedge; in a chronic non-healing ulcer biopsy is mandatory rather than optional, because SRB's rule for chronic wounds is that they are "unresponsive to dressing treatment; it requires biopsy, culture study, definitive treatment like wound debridement, VAC therapy, skin grafting or flap".​SRB 1 · p.4
Discharge for culture, and for acid-fast bacilli
SRB's sequence in a tuberculous ulcer is discharge study, biopsy, then antituberculous drugs.​SRB 1 · p.17
Vascular assessment
Ankle-brachial pressure index and duplex, because you must know the arterial supply before you compress a venous ulcer or graft anything.
Blood glucose, HbA1c and sensation testing
For the diabetic and neuropathic foot.
Radiograph of the underlying bone
If the base is bone, for osteomyelitis or a sequestrum, which is also a cause of a persistent sinus.​SRB 1 · p.31

5Treatment, in principle

Treat the cause, not the hole
The ulcer is a symptom. A venous ulcer needs the venous hypertension treated; an arterial ulcer needs revascularisation; a neuropathic ulcer needs offloading; a tuberculous ulcer needs drugs. SRB's instruction for a venous ulcer is explicit: once granulating, graft it, and undertake a definitive procedure for the varicose veins after evaluation.​SRB 1 · p.18
Prepare the bed
Debridement, control of infection, and vacuum-assisted closure where available.​SRB 1 · p.4 Scoop out proud flesh with a Volkmann's scoop before grafting, and look for the foreign body that caused it.​SRB 1 · p.19
Then close it
Skin grafting once there is healthy granulation, or a flap where the base is bone or tendon.​SRB 1 · p.4, p.18
If it is malignant
Wide local excision with skin grafting,​SRB 1 · p.24 and for a basal cell carcinoma note B&L's technique for difficult sites: Mohs' micrographic surgery, developed by Mohs in 1938 for cutaneous malignant lesions.​B&L 45 · p.652
Rodent ulcer, in one paragraph SRB: "It is the ulcerative form of basal cell carcinoma which is common in the face."​SRB 1 · p.24 B&L: a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour of pluripotential epithelial cells arising from basal epidermis and hair follicles, so it affects pilosebaceous skin; the risk factor is ultraviolet radiation; 90% are nodular or nodular cystic, and it is divided into high- and low-risk BCC.​B&L 45 · p.651 The edge is raised, beaded and pearly-white.​SRB 1 · p.15 It is locally invasive and does not metastasise, which is why it is called rodent: it gnaws.

6Rapid-fire viva

Define an ulcer, and name its parts.

A disruption or break in the continuity of any lining, whether skin, mucous membrane or other, and one of the types of wound.​SRB 1 · p.1 Its parts are the margin, the edge, the floor and the base.​SRB 1 · p.15 The margin is the junction with normal skin, the edge lies between margin and floor, the floor is what you see, and the base is what the ulcer rests on and must be palpated.​Das 4 · p.64

Name the types of edge and what each means.

Sloping: healing, with red granulation centrally, then a blue zone of growing epithelium, then white scar. Undermined: tuberculous, because the disease advances in the deeper plane while the epidermis proliferates inwards, so a probe passes between edge and floor. Punched out: gummatous or trophic, from endarteritis. Raised, beaded and pearly-white: rodent ulcer, that is basal cell carcinoma. Everted or rolled out: squamous cell carcinoma, because the ulcer heaps up and spills over normal skin. And the inflamed, irregular, oedematous edge of a spreading ulcer.​SRB 1 · p.15, p.16​Das 4 · p.63, p.64

Why is a tuberculous ulcer's edge undermined?

Because the disease process advances in the deeper plane, in the subcutaneous tissue, while the epidermis proliferates inwards over it, leaving the skin edge overhanging an undermined cavity.​SRB 1 · p.15 The bedside proof is that a probe can be insinuated easily between the edge and the floor.​Das 4 · p.63

Why is a gummatous ulcer punched out?

Endarteritis.​SRB 1 · p.15 The tissue dies in a block because its blood supply dies, so the edge drops vertically rather than sloping or being undermined. The same mechanism gives the punched-out edge of a trophic ulcer.

Distinguish a spreading from a healing ulcer.

Spreading: inflamed, irregular, oedematous edge; floor with absent or unhealthy granulation, profuse purulent discharge and slough; red oedematous surroundings; regional nodes enlarged and tender; acutely painful. Healing: sloping edge; healthy pink or red granulation with scanty serous discharge and no slough; no surrounding inflammation; and nodes that may be enlarged but are always non-tender.​SRB 1 · p.16 The tenderness of the nodes is the cleanest discriminator.

What does pale flat granulation tissue mean? And proud flesh?

Unhealthy, pale, flat granulation means a chronic non-healing or callous ulcer. Exuberant granulation, proud flesh, protrudes out of the ulcer bed or sinus opening like a proliferating mass, and is commonly associated with a retained foreign body; it should be scooped out with a Volkmann's scoop before grafting. A pyogenic granuloma is a type of it, presenting as a well-localised red swelling that bleeds on touching.​SRB 1 · p.19 So proud flesh should make you look for a foreign body.

Where would you biopsy, and why not the floor?

From the edge, including a margin of adjacent normal skin, because the edge is where the active disease is and where the architecture that gives the diagnosis survives. The floor is slough and granulation tissue and will not be diagnostic. In a chronic non-healing ulcer biopsy is mandatory, along with culture, since chronic wounds unresponsive to dressings require biopsy and culture before definitive treatment.​SRB 1 · p.4

Where is a venous ulcer, and where is it never?

Around the ankle in the gaiter's zone, vertically oval, commonly on the medial side, occasionally lateral, sometimes both, but never above the middle third of the leg.​SRB 1 · p.27 It is due to ambulatory chronic venous hypertension, from saphenous or perforator incompetence or a post-phlebitic limb, and it is initially painful but becomes painless with chronicity.

A painless ulcer on the ball of the foot. What is it and what must you test?

A trophic or neuropathic ulcer, at a site of maximum weight bearing, which S Das places on the heel or ball of the foot.​Das 4 · p.63 Test sensation, and look for the cause of the neuropathy: diabetes, leprosy, or a nerve injury whose scar may be visible.​Das 4 · p.63​B&L 6 · p.80 Its edge is punched out, from endarteritis.

What is Marjolin's ulcer, and does it metastasise?

A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing unstable scar, classically a burn scar or after snake bite. The classical teaching is that it is well differentiated and does not spread by lymphatics or blood, because the scar is relatively avascular and alymphatic, so there is no early route for spread.​SRB 1 · p.24 But Bailey and Love 28e simply defines it as an SCC in a scar and makes no exception for its behaviour.​B&L 45 · p.652 So treat it as a squamous carcinoma with wide local excision and grafting, and follow the nodes rather than assume they are safe, because once it grows beyond the scar into vascularised tissue it can metastasise.

What is a rodent ulcer?

The ulcerative form of basal cell carcinoma,​SRB 1 · p.24 common on the face: a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour of pluripotential epithelial cells arising from basal epidermis and hair follicles, so it affects pilosebaceous skin; ultraviolet radiation is the risk factor and 90% are nodular or nodular cystic.​B&L 45 · p.651 Its edge is raised, beaded and pearly-white. It is locally invasive and does not metastasise, hence rodent: it gnaws. For difficult sites, Mohs' micrographic surgery.

What is induration and where is it best felt?

A palpatory sign meaning a specific type of hardness in the diseased tissue, obvious in well-differentiated carcinomas and best felt in squamous cell carcinoma.​SRB 1 · p.15 Palpate the base and the margin between finger and thumb and report it separately from the edge.

Classify ulcers pathologically.

Specific: tuberculous, syphilitic, actinomycotic. Malignant: carcinomatous, rodent, melanotic. Non-specific: traumatic, which may be mechanical, physical or chemical and is the commonest; arterial, from atherosclerosis or thromboangiitis obliterans; venous or gravitational; trophic or neuropathic; and the ulcers of systemic disease including anaemia, polycythaemia, sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, leukaemia, vasculitis and autoimmune disease.​SRB 1 · p.17, p.29

How would you treat a chronic non-healing ulcer?

Treat the cause, not the hole. Biopsy and culture it first, because chronic wounds unresponsive to dressings need both. Then debride, control infection, and use vacuum-assisted closure where available; scoop out proud flesh and look for a retained foreign body. Close it with a skin graft once healthy granulation appears, or a flap if the base is bone or tendon. And deal with the underlying cause: the venous hypertension, the arterial supply, the offloading, the glycaemic control, or the antituberculous drugs.​SRB 1 · p.4, p.18, p.19

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, skin and subcutaneous tissue is chapter 45 and tropical infections and infestations chapter 6; the ulcer material in the Indian texts is S Das ch.4 and SRB ch.1, and almost all of the classical edge and floor description is theirs.
